The manuscript, edited by Pu Maozuo 濮茅左, comprises only fifty- eight slips, corresponding to just about 36% (thirty- four hexagrams in total) of the received Zhouyi. \(^{3}\) From a structural standpoint, this manuscript is very similar to the Fuyang version: the hexagram picture, which is visually divided into two trigrams, is located at the top of the slip. As we shall see, this aspect is also present in the Shifa manuscript, which hypothetically belongs to the same cultural

area (the State of Chu) and the same historical period (mid- to late \(4^{\text{th}}\) century BCE).<sup>1</sup> The hexagram picture is immediately followed by the hexagram name—although with several graphic and lexical variants typical of the Chu script—the hexagram statement and the line statement. A few mysterious symbols are interpolated between these parts of the texts. Scholars have used them to reconstruct the hexagram sequence. I shall not delve too much into the details of this process. For the purposes of the present discussion, suffice it to say that, apparently, the sequence of the Shanghai Museum might be the same as the received one.<sup>2</sup>  

The last manuscript version was exhumed from the grave of the Marquis of Haihun 海昏侯 (Nanchang 南昌, Jiangxi 江西) in 2015. Among many grave goods belonging to the tomb occupant, a large corpus of manuscripts has been found, including yet another version of the Zhouyi which also dates to the beginning of the Western Han period. The text is written on sixty- four strips (i.e. one hexagram per each strip), and while the hexagram sequence is the same as the received one, the text following each hexagram is remarkably different.<sup>3</sup> One aspect which is worth mentioning as it is relevant to our discussion of the shuzi gua is that the hexagram pictures are not written with numbers (1 and 8) but with the more common broken and unbroken lines. This once again proves that the hexagram pictures were not visually standardised until the early Western Han.  

Finally, it is worth mentioning one last manuscript. In 1993, in the village of Wangjiatai 王家台, Hubei 湖北, inside the Tomb 15 (one of the sixteen tombs opened by some workers while digging a fish pond) archaeologists found a set of mantic tools, such as dice, wooden diviner's board, bamboo

sorting stalks, as well as the only authentic pre- imperial version of the Guicang, a different divination manual long thought to be lost, or regarded as a late forgery.  

Another somewhat related manuscript comes from the collection of looted texts purchased by Tsinghua University, called by the editors Biegua别卦 (Hexagrams). This manuscript consists of the hexagram sequence without text attached to each hexagram picture. The sequence is the same as the one found in the Mawangdui manuscript; however, for some reason the scribe(s) decided to write only the upper trigrams. Interestingly, unlike the other manuscript versions of the Zhouyi, the so- called broken line is written with the number 6 and not 8. Therefore, on this aspect, it bears a resemblance with the Shifa manuscript, which I shall discuss later in this chapter, as well as the dagger- axe which probably dates to the late Western Zhou period (see my Analytical Map for more details on this object). Lastly, the hexagrams names are also quite different.  

What can we gain from the analysis of these manuscripts? To be sure, different traditions which differed mainly in the way they depicted the broken line (either using 6 or 8), the hexagram and trigram order, as well as the names of the hexagrams coexisted until the mid \(2^{\text{nd}}\) century BCE. The text attached to each hexagram, when present, is quite consistent with the received tradition, and achieved its definitive shape by no later than the 300 BCE. Most importantly, the moral- philosophical aspect and the divinatory ones were still present until at least the early Western Han. The Fuyang manuscript in particular ‘confirms that the Zhouyi developed in the context of divination’ and the ‘humanistic rationale’ was attached to it much later than the orthodox exegetic tradition had claimed for centuries. Furthermore, Edward Shaughnessy, in his study on the unearthed Changes, remarks that the text was widespread in different kingdoms of the Warring

Also most Chinese publications for example on the Mawangdui Yijing assume that there was only one correct version of the Yijing and normally present differences between the transmitted and the excavated text as mistakes or loan- graphs appearing in the latter.<sup>121</sup> Hertzler criticises this approach and argues that it was questionable if the 'creation' of one 'correct' version of the Yijing did justice to its function as a book of divination.<sup>122</sup> Western methods of textual critique that rely on the criteria of Folgefehler to construct a stemma codicum of the different versions, are not that easy applicable to such texts, even more so because they do not allow for lateral contamination across the branches or for instances of non- written textual re- production in between.  

In an article called "The difficulty of the Yijing", Smith names two main reasons for the elusiveness of the meaning of this text: the non- linguistic signs, the hexagrams, that were created to make clear what human language is unable to express, and the "lack of 'syntax'" that rendered the meaning cryptic already at an early point of transmission history.<sup>123</sup> Furthermore, the interpretation of the divination outcome was situationally bound due to the ambiguity of the Yi and "its longevity as a tool of divination is due in part to the elusiveness of its meaning," as Smith holds.<sup>124</sup> Also Dominique Hertzler argues: "Anders als bei religiösen oder ideologischen Texten, die von der Authentizität des richigen Wortes leben, entfaltet sich die Bedeutung eines Orakelbuches erst durch
...
die Polysemie der einzelnen Worte wie des gesamten Textes."125 A search for the sense, the intended word and the graph that renders it most correctly therefore does not make much sense. Transmitted sources on divination have furthermore shown that diviners could modify the statements they found in divination handbooks or even create new ones.126 These can again have entered into the texts themselves, changed them and induced the development of several transmission traditions. Therefore there is not the Yijing or the Guicang that can be reconstructed from the extant textual witnesses according to Western ideas of an urtext.  

To face the problem of the great fluidity of lexicon, writing and text, and to do justice to the different text types, Kern suggested to "establish a distributional pattern of types of variants that appear at the manuscript at hand."127 Along those lines, Hertzer developed an unfortunately unpublished research guide to the Mawangdui Yijing that tries to determine the exact lexical definition of all meanings of a given graph, contrasts the diverging characters and points out similarities and differences in meaning.128 Undertakings like this as well as studies in phonology, etymology and grammar are the absolutely necessary basis for all further investigations on the various Yi.  

Beyond that, it is unclear how to do justice to the broad range of possible meanings when editing a text. For translations, be they in modern Chinese or Western languages, the problem is even greater and the authors most of the time decide for only one reading or - for Chinese- Chinese translations - simply choose one character without further discussions on its meaning or the reasons for their choice. To reconstruct single stages of textual transmission, i.e., different editions and versions, and to confront them in a critical edition remains a goal that for the Yijing might be reached within the next decades. For the Guicang with its much more unfavorable material basis unfortunately much less preliminary studies or comparisons have been made, but even here systematic analysis and editing should allow for producing a critical edition that can be used for further research on divination methods and manuals.

At the same time, it has become clear that a systematic approach can go far in making sense of this problematic textual heritage. In five steps, starting from definitions and the history and preconceptions of previous traditions of textual criticism in both China and the West, the paper then investigated processes and mechanisms of textual (re)production before comparing excavated and transmitted texts and finally combining all of these insights in a general textual critique. Applied to the example of the Guicang, this approach has shown that the question of the authenticity of the Chinese textual heritage remains rather problematic should rather be supplanted by detailed

reconstructions of various strands of textual development, research that needs to combine the different strands of evidence discussed throughout this paper.

Finally, the early \(Yi\) system Q may not have had hexagram names assigned based on its hexagram and line statements until the early Spring and Autumn period. Once these hexagram names were established, it is possible that the later \(Yi\) traditions from the mid- Warring States period duplicated the hexagram names from the early \(Yi\) system Q through the commonly used hexagram and line pictures. By the

mid- Warring States period, these hexagram names diverged into two distinct systems: the Guicang and Zhouyi lineages. This chapter will now explore the hexagram names used by the Zhouyi and Guicang lineages, as shown in Appendix III, from the mid- Warring States period to the early Western Han. Regarding the Zhouyi lineage Q1, its hexagram names may have originated from the early Yi system Q. Consequently, the hexagram names of Q1 appear to be more intentional, systematic, distinguishable, and stable across its various transmitting lines. Despite some textual differences, such as loan and variant characters, the hexagram names from various sources have maintained consistency along a single transmitting line. The Zhouyi's hexagram names found on Shanghai Museum bamboo slips should be older than those on the Mawangdui silk manuscripts, Shuangqudui bamboo strips, wooden strips discovered from the tomb of the Marquis of Haihun, and the received version. The names of their hexagrams varied primarily because they were passed down through different lineages. It is also interesting to note the similarities between the hexagram names of the Zhouyi Q1 and Guicang Q2 lineages. For example, the hexagram names of the Zhouyi found in the Mawangdui silk manuscripts, Shuangqudui bamboo strips, and wooden strips discovered from the tomb of the Marquis of Haihun align closely with those of the received Zhouyi. Furthermore, some of the hexagram names closely resemble those found in the Biegua from the Tsinghua bamboo slips and the Guicang from the Shuangqudui bamboo strips. The Zhouyi from the Mawangdui silk manuscripts and Shuangqudui bamboo strips were recorded during the reign of the Han emperor Wen 文 (r. 180–157 BCE), which indicates that they were made before the later convergence of the various Yi systems. Therefore, they likely upheld the Zhouyi's form during the late Warring States period and throughout the Qin- Han era (He 2025: 21). Moreover, the hexagram names found in the Yizhan discovered from the tomb of the Marquis of Haihun derive from the earlier form of the Zhouyi before its finalization. Thus, it indicates a transitional stage during that period (Zhu 2020: 254–266).  

As far as the Guicang lineage Q2 is concerned, it appears that its hexagram names may have originated from the ancient Zhouyi's hexagram names.
...
there is no clear distinction among different transmitting lines. Additionally, the hexagram names of Q2 reflect various naming conventions from earlier times, suggesting that they are relatively old. Specifically, the hexagram names found in the Shifa and Biegua from the Tsinghua bamboo slips are likely older than those in the Wangjiatai bamboo strips and the recollected Guicang. A plausible explanation for the hexagram names of the Guicang lineage Q2 is that they may have been copied from the hexagram names used in the early Zhouyi lineage Q1 and then evolved independently through different transmission lines. Consequently, the hexagram names of the Guicang from the Shuanggudui bamboo strips and the recollected Guicang generally correspond to those in the received Zhouyi, although there are some notable differences. The hexagram names in the recollected Guicang show textual affinities of both the Guicang Q2 and Zhouyi Q1 lineages. The similarities in hexagram names across various Yi lineages highlight the complex origins and transmission of these names, likely due to the convergence of Yi systems in the early Western Han period (He 2025: 31- 32).

In the first two stages, this chapter has examined how the Zhouyi and Guicang originated from a single source: an early Yi system known as Q. Over time, they developed into two distinct divination systems: the Zhouyi Q1 and Guicang Q2 lineages. In this third stage, this chapter will discuss how the final versions of the Zhouyi Q1 and Guicang Q2 lineages evolved from those earlier manuscripts. Let us take the case of the sources analysed in the present thesis as an example. The shuzi gua materials reflect a diversity and complexity which does not in any way exclude the presence of abstract thought. The numerological evidence suggests that early Chinese people, living across quite an extended area, were very much capable of thinking in terms of modules and odd- even numbers very early on, even though I would not link this to a proto- Yin- Yang mentality. Therefore, the shift described in this thesis is a conceptual one. If we look at the Xici, it appears clear that the text is not concerned with giving explicit definitions of the concepts it mentions. For instance, we are not told what 'easiness' and 'simplicity' are, we must infer the meanings of these two crucial concepts by ourselves. As I have mentioned at the beginning of this chapter, the Xici takes for granted that all these meanings are familiar to the text recipient(s) because they are entirely consistent with the worldview dominant during the periods in which the text was being con

ceived by multiple authors (5<sup>th</sup>- 3<sup>rd</sup> century BCE). The sixty- four hexagrams—which purportedly stem from the numerical progression 1, 2, 4, 8, 64—ultimately corresponds to the ‘myriad things’ (wanwu 萬物), which is the way most philosophical texts, mainly belonging to the so- called Daoist tradition, refer to the ‘multiplicity of reality.’<sup>1</sup> Indeed, the Zhouyi, far from being the product of the sages of the past, ‘emerged from a world of diverse but related practices that fundamentally shaped it.’<sup>2</sup> What was most likely the outcome of a stochastic distribution was given philosophical legitimacy,<sup>3</sup> ultimately establishing a credible cosmo- philosophical framework for the numerological system of one of the many divination manuals in 3<sup>rd</sup> century BCE China. If read in this way, the endeavour of the authors of the Xici appears even more remarkable.  

Let us now turn to what are arguably the two most important features of the whole Yi tradition, namely the correspondence of the odd numbers with the Yang lines and the even numbers with the Yin lines. This is indeed correct, and the earliest indisputable evidence for this comes from the dagger- axe and the pottery handles first and was then confirmed by the Shifa and the Biegua. These two main traditions, which for ease of argument, I shall refer to as the shuzi gua traditions and the Yi traditions, were parallel. The Warring States manuscript versions of the Zhouyi and the Warring States divinatory records make plain this aspect. Therefore, both the Guicang manuscript and the recollected version may have circulated as divination texts during the Warring States period, and later been adapted into the form of the Zhouyi. In conclusion, the records found in the transmitted documents of the Guicang correspond to both the unearthed manuscript and the recollected version. This correspondence illustrates how the Guicang lineage has endured throughout Chinese history (Jia 2020: 34; Xin 2017: 47; Zheng 2016: 37- 72; Cheng 2015: 42; He 2025: 21).  

As discussed above, archaeological finds over the last five decades indicate that numerous Yi traditions existed in early China. Studies of the various divination methods used by the early Yi system of numerical- line hexagrams suggest that the Zhouyi and Guicang were two separate divination systems that originated from a common source but evolved into distinct streams. Because the two kinds of Guicang texts may have been composed in the shape of the Zhouyi, the Zhouyi and the Guicang likely influenced each other during their development. Although many received documents include references to Zhouyi, this chapter will avoid concluding that all transmitted and unearthed materials belong to a single Zhouyi tradition. Instead, to gain a better understanding of the Zhouyi, it is essential to adopt a more nuanced view that also takes the Guicang into account.  

According to the method of historical criticism, this chapter puts forward a

threefold method—the single- source, double- lineage, and three- stage system—to trace the development of the Zhouyi. \(^{12}\) Stage one focuses on the textual formation of the Zhouyi. From the late Shang dynasty to the early Spring and Autumn period, the numerical- line hexagrams constituted an early Yi system, which should be regarded as a preliminary version. Due to the deficiency of relevant transmitted and excavated materials, it is unclear whether another source, referred to as S, existed. As a result, the early Yi system can be considered a single source, Q, which served as the common textual source for the later Zhouyi Q1 and Guicang Q2 lineages. Stage two addresses the textual evolution of the Zhouyi from the mid- Warring States period to the early Western Han era. During this time, the early Yi system Q further split into the Zhouyi Q1 and Guicang Q2 lineages. These two lineages evolved to include a variety of texts, some of which have likely been recently discovered by Chinese archaeologists. These texts should be recognized as representing an intermediate stage. Stage three marks the period when the Zhouyi text was finalized. As far as the Zhouyi lineage Q1 is

concerned, it shows a textual kinship that is quite close to the early Yi system Q. During the reigns of the Han emperors Wu and Xuan, Q1 by and large reached its final form as the received Zhouyi. In contrast, only fragments of the Guicang lineage Q2 have survived, recollected by Qing dynasty scholars, resulting in a recompilation of a fragmentary Guicang text. Compared to the interaction between the two lineages found in the intermediate versions of Zhouyi lineage Q1 from the early Western Han period, the compilation of the recollected Guicang shows a more significant incorporation from both lineages. This results in particularly complex textual affinities and relationships.<sup>13</sup>  

## Stage One: The early Yi system of numerical-line hexagrams  

The Zhouyi, which was used for divination concerning state affairs and royal life, was an essential part of the intellectual and social fabric of Zhou China. Once a numerical- line hexagram was determined through various divination methods, the corresponding hexagram and line statements served to clarify the divination results. According to the auspicious or inauspicious predictions, those for whom the hexagram was generated would attempt to act accordingly. Milfoil divination, a divination method used in the Zhouyi, likely dates back to the Shang dynasty. Turtle- shell divination, which predates milfoil divination, must have profoundly influenced its formation and utilization. Thus, the line statements in the Zhouyi evolved in the same intellectual environment as turtle- shell divination.

The third topic to explore involves the hexagram and line statements of the early Yi system Q. According to the Xici, the Zhouyi was composed during the conflicts between King Wen and the tyrant Zhou 封 (1105- 1046 BCE). It began to flourish in the middle period of Chinese antiquity, specifically during the final period of the

Shang dynasty, when the influence of the future Zhou dynasty began to emerge (Wang Bi, Han Kangbo, and Kong Yingda eds., Songben Zhouyi zhushu, 457, 466). Traditionally, the composition of the Zhouyi has been attributed to King Wen of Zhou. Since it is impossible to know for certain whether he was directly involved, it has to remain a speculation that the composition occurred during his era, specifically during the transition from the Shang to the Zhou dynasty.\(^{22}\) However, the Zhouyi also records some historical events that took place after the time of King Wen. Consequently, some Han Confucian scholars, such as Ma Rong 馬融 (79- 166) and Lu Ji 陸續 (188- 219), contended that while King Wen authored the statements regarding the image of the hexagrams, it was the Duke of Zhou 周公 (1042- 1035 BCE) who wrote the line statements (Wang Bi, Han Kangbo, and Kong Yingda eds., Songben Zhouyi zhushu, 14- 15). Scholars in China widely agree that the Zhouyi was created during the early Western Zhou period (Liao 2004: 177- 178).\(^{23}\) In Western

scholarship, there are differing perspectives on the Zhouyi.24 Additionally, another question arises concerning the hexagram and line statements used by the early Yi system Q. Regarding the excavated materials, a dagger- axe from the turn of the two Zhou dynasties is the earliest known vessel to feature an inscription of any hexagram and line statements, specifically the hexagram Ding. This artifact represents the first instance of a combination of hexagram and line pictures, as well as statements discovered so far. The inscription can be transcribed and translated as follows (Shaughnessy 2022: 35- 36):  

6- 1- 1- 1- 6- 1 says: The cauldron's legs overturned. The cauldron's yellow ears; setting down its legs. 8- 5- 1- 1- 6- 5 Stinted  

六一—六一曰鼎止（趾）真（颠）鼎黄耳奠止（趾）八五一—六五拇（吝）  

Notably, its inscription of the hexagram Ding's statement only partially corresponds to later Guicang's fragments collected in the Tang encyclopedia, Yiwen leiju 藝文類聚 (Collection of Literature Arranged by Categories), as follows:  

Divine with the Guicang, saying: "The caldron has yellow ears; it is auspicious to

obtain sturgeons."  

《归藏》占曰：鼎有黄耳，利得鲤鲤。(Jia 2020: 202- 203)  

Moreover, it also corresponds to the received Zhouyi as follows:  

First Six: A caldron's upturned legs: Beneficial to expel the bad, Getting a consort with her child. Without trouble.  

初六：鼎颠趾。利出否。得妄以其子。无咎。  

Six in the Fifth: A caldron's yellow ears and metal bar. Beneficial to affirm.  

六五：鼎黄耳金铉。利贞。

Thus, there are significant textual differences when comparing the early Yi system Q with the Zhouyi Q1 and Guicang Q2 lineages. Readers should approach this text cautiously, as the available textual evidence may reveal only minor textual affinities. These similarities do not prove that the hexagram and line statements of the early Yi system Q were finished during the Zhou period. In conclusion, based on the earliest excavated materials, it appears that around the transition between the two Zhou dynasties, the hexagram and line statements used by the early Yi system Q had not yet reached the final form as found in the later Zhouyi or Guicang lineages. However, the received Zhouyi and Guicang texts may have originated from an earlier version of the Yi system Q, as indicated by texts such as the hexagram Ding inscribed on the dagger- axe.

Notes: The earliest extant copy of the Changes is part of the Shanghai Museum collection of bamboo strips, dated to approximately 300-278 BCE and illegally excavated in the early 1990s from a site in Jingmen, Hubei province (for more on this find, see the entry by Sarah Allan on the Rongchengshi). This version of the Changes consists of almost fifty- eight bamboo strips or fragments and contains thirty- four hexagrams and 1,806 characters (approximately one third of the the received text without commentaries). In general, this version resembles the received text save for the the fact that two trigrams of each hexagram are somewhat separated and it features six different kinds of black or red square symbols that appear immediately after the hexagram names (Smith 2008, 49- 50). As well, a number of bamboo fragments were unearthed from a Qin (221- 206 BCE) tomb at Wangjiatai in Hubei province in 1993. These fragments correspond to the Guicang, one of the three versions of the Zhouyi mentioned in the Zhouli and preserved in fragmentary form in the collections of Ma Guohan (1794- 1857) and Hong Yixuan (1765- 1837). Many of the hexagrams within these excavated materials conform to the received Changes, while some of them match the hexagrams in the Mawangdui Changes that differ from the received Changes (Smith 2008, 48- 49). Finally, the so- called Fuyang materials (excavated from the tomb of Lord Xiaohou Zao in 1977 at Shuanggudui in Anhui province) contain 750 bamboo fragments that correspond to the received Changes. The tomb is dated to 165 BCE. The Fuyang materials also contain other divinatory material associated with the "day books" (rishu 日書) of the Han period, suggesting that it may have been a distinct work produced within the same divinatory context as the Zhouyi (Smith 2008, 49). In addition, the Shifa 签法 ("Stalk Method") is a recently discovered text also written on bamboo. The Shifa is part of the collection of bamboo texts purchased by Tsinghua University in 2008 and it is possible

that it influenced the development of the Changes. For a full discussion, see Smith Forthcoming.

Notes: A silk manuscript of the Changes was excavated at Mawangdui in Hunan province in 1970 and has been dated to approximately 190 BCE. Significantly, this manuscript features a different ordering of the hexagrams, different names for several of the hexagrams, and unique commentaries. For more on these differences, see the note on "Are there multiple versions of the text" below (Smith 2008, 50- 56). It is also undoubtedly the case that there exist other fragments of the Changes written on silk that have yet to be discovered.
